chapters.title: Writing Basics: What Makes a Good Sentence?

sections.title: Sentence Writing
learningObjectives: Identify the components of a basic sentence.
Identify the four most serious writing errors.
sections.content:
Complete sentences require three things: a **subject**, a **verb**, and a **complete idea**.

## Subjects

The subject tells who or what the sentence is about. Subjects are nouns or pronouns. A **compound subject** has two or more nouns joined by *and*, *or*, or *nor*. A **prepositional phrase** can never be the subject.

## Verbs

- **Action verbs** show action: *She submits the report.*
- **Linking verbs** connect subject to description: *The memo is clear.*
- **Helping verbs** work with main verbs: *He has finished the draft.*

## Sentence Patterns

| Pattern | Example |
|---------|----------|
| S-V | Sales increased. |
| S-LV-N | Maria is a director. |
| S-LV-Adj | The proposal seems solid. |
| S-V-DO | She sent the invoice. |

## Fragments and Run-ons

A **fragment** is missing a subject or verb: *Waiting for approval.* Fix: *We are waiting for approval.*

**Run-on types:**
- **Fused sentence** (no punctuation): *The report was late we missed the deadline.*
- **Comma splice** (only a comma): *The report was late, we missed the deadline.*

**Four fixes:** period | semicolon | comma + FANBOYS (for/and/nor/but/or/yet/so) | dependent word (because/although/since/unless)

keyTerms.definition: Words with subject and verb that stand alone as a complete thought.
Incomplete sentence missing subject or verb.
Two or more independent clauses incorrectly combined.
Two complete sentences joined with no punctuation.
Two complete sentences joined only by a comma.
FANBOYS: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so.
Begins with a preposition; cannot be the subject.
Verb showing what the subject does.
Verb connecting subject to noun or adjective (is, seem, appear).
Works with main verb to show tense or mood (be, do, have).

exercises.instruction: Underline subjects and circle prepositional phrases.
items: The gym closes at nine tonight.
We went to the store to buy supplies.
The student with the highest grade won the award.

exercises.instruction: Underline the verb twice and name its type.
items: The memo sounds urgent.
They have not responded yet.
She drafted the proposal in one afternoon.

keyTakeaways: A sentence needs subject, verb, and complete thought.
Prepositional phrases cannot be subjects.
Fix fragments by adding missing parts.
Fix run-ons with period, semicolon, FANBOYS, or dependent word.

sections.title: Subject-Verb Agreement
sections.content:
Subject and verb must **agree in number**.

## Regular Verbs

Third-person singular adds -s: *She writes.* / *They write.*

## Irregular Verbs

| Verb | Singular | Plural |
|------|----------|--------|
| be | am/is/are | are |
| have | have/has | have |
| do | do/does | do |

## Common Agreement Errors

**AND** = plural: *Maria and David attend the meeting.*
**OR/NOR** = verb agrees with nearest: *Neither the manager nor the assistants are available.*
**Indefinite pronouns** (everyone, nobody, each) = singular.
**Collective nouns** (team, committee) = singular in American English.
**Here/There sentences**: subject follows verb — *Here are the results.*

keyTerms.definition: Subject and verb must match in number.
Verb with unpredictable forms (be, have, do).
Unspecified person/thing, usually singular (everyone, each, nobody).
Names a group treated as one unit — takes singular verb.

exercises.instruction: Write the correct present-tense verb form.
items: The committee (meet/meets) every Thursday.
Everyone (is/are) required to submit a report.
My dog and cat (chases/chase) each other.

keyTakeaways: Singular subjects take singular verbs; plural take plural.
Compound subjects with AND take plural verbs.
Collective nouns take singular verbs in American English.

sections.title: Verb Tense
learningObjectives: Use correct regular and irregular verb tenses.
sections.content:
Verb tense identifies **when** an action occurs.

## Regular Verbs

Add -ed/-d for simple past: *walk -> walked, present -> presented*

## Irregular Verbs

| Present | Past |
|---------|------|
| be | was/were |
| have | had |
| go | went |
| see | saw |
| write | wrote |
| know | knew |

## Consistent Verb Tense

Use the same tense throughout unless a real time shift occurs.

**Inconsistent:** *She opened the file and types the data.*
**Consistent:** *She opened the file and typed the data.*

keyTerms.definition: Form of verb indicating when action occurs.
Forms past tense by adding -ed or -d.
Unpredictable past form that must be memorized.
Using the same tense throughout a sentence or paragraph.

exercises.instruction: Select the correct tense.
items: The Dust Bowl (is/was) devastating in the 1930s.
Historians (consider/considered) it one of the worst events in US history.

keyTakeaways: Regular verbs add -ed for past.
Irregular verb past forms must be memorized.
Consistent tense is essential for clarity.

sections.title: Capitalization
learningObjectives: Learn the basic rules of capitalization.
sections.content:
## Rules

**Capitalize:**
- First word of every sentence
- Proper nouns (Amazon River, Dr. Patel, Smith College, Tuesday, March, Thanksgiving)
- Nationalities, races, languages, religions (American, Spanish, Catholic, Buddhist)
- Titles before names (Dr. Smith, President Lincoln)
- Days, months, holidays

**Do NOT capitalize** common nouns used generally: *river*, *doctor*, *college*.

## ALL CAPS = Shouting

In digital communication, ALL CAPS implies yelling. Use standard capitalization.

| Incorrect | Correct |
|-----------|---------|
| the amazon river | the Amazon River |
| dr. johnson | Dr. Johnson |
| she is catholic | She is Catholic |

keyTerms.definition: Name of a specific person, place, or organization — always capitalized.
General word for a class — not capitalized.

exercises.instruction: Correct capitalization errors.
items: the prince of england enjoys polo.
my physician, dr. alvarez, makes me comfortable.
i am taking english, history, and biology.

keyTakeaways: Capitalize first word, proper nouns, nationalities, titles before names.
ALL CAPS implies shouting — avoid in professional writing.

sections.title: Pronouns
sections.content:
Pronouns must agree with their **antecedent** in number and person.

**Singular:** *The manager submitted **her** report.*
**Indefinite pronouns are singular:** everyone, nobody, each, someone
**Collective nouns are singular:** *The team completed **its** project.*

## Subject vs. Object Pronouns

| Role | Pronouns |
|------|----------|
| Subject | I, we, you, he, she, it, they |
| Object | me, us, you, him, her, it, them |

**Incorrect:** *Me and Harriet went to the meeting.*
**Correct:** *Harriet and I went to the meeting.*

## Who vs. Whom

*Who* = subject: *Who submitted the report?*
*Whom* = object: *To whom should I address this?*
Trick: If 'him' fits, use 'whom'.

keyTerms.definition: Word replacing a noun.
The noun a pronoun refers to.
Pronoun must match antecedent in number and person.
I, we, you, he, she, it, they.
me, us, you, him, her, it, them.

exercises.instruction: Correct the pronoun errors.
items: Everyone should submit their timesheet by Friday.
The award was given to he and I.
Me and the director presented the findings.

keyTakeaways: Pronouns must agree with antecedent in number and person.
Most indefinite pronouns are singular.
Who = subject; whom = object.

sections.title: Adjectives and Adverbs
sections.content:
**Adjective** describes a noun or pronoun: *The **detailed** report impressed the client.*

**Adverb** describes a verb, adjective, or adverb (often ends in -ly): *She presented **confidently**.*

## Comparative and Superlative

- Comparative (2 things): -er or *more*
- Superlative (3+ things): -est or *most*

| Word | Comparative | Superlative |
|------|-------------|-------------|
| good/well | better | best |
| bad/badly | worse | worst |

## Good vs. Well / Bad vs. Badly

*Good* and *bad* are **adjectives**. *Well* and *badly* are **adverbs**.

**Incorrect:** *She did good on the exam.*
**Correct:** *She did **well** on the exam.*

keyTerms.definition: Describes a noun or pronoun.
Describes a verb, adjective, or adverb; often ends in -ly.
Compares two things; add -er or use more.
Compares three or more; add -est or use most.

exercises.instruction: Write good, well, bad, or badly.
items: She performed ________ under pressure.
The results looked ________ for investors.

exercises.instruction: Write the correct comparative or superlative.
items: This proposal is ________ (good) than the last one.

keyTakeaways: Adjectives describe nouns; adverbs describe verbs/adjectives/adverbs.
Comparative compares two; superlative compares three or more.
Good/bad are adjectives; well/badly are adverbs.

sections.title: Misplaced and Dangling Modifiers
learningObjectives: Identify and correct misplaced and dangling modifiers.
sections.content:
## Misplaced Modifiers

A **misplaced modifier** is too far from the word it describes.

**Incorrect:** *She wore a helmet on her head that was too large.*
**Correct:** *She wore a helmet that was too large on her head.*

Watch for: *only, almost, just, nearly, barely*
**Confusing:** *He almost earned fifty dollars.*
**Clear:** *He earned almost fifty dollars.*

## Dangling Modifiers

A **dangling modifier** describes something not present in the sentence.

**Incorrect:** *Reviewing the budget, the numbers seemed off.*
**Correct:** *Reviewing the budget, she noticed the numbers seemed off.*

Three-step check: (1) Find the -ing phrase. (2) Underline the first noun after it. (3) Ask: does that noun logically perform the action?

keyTerms.definition: Word, phrase, or clause clarifying another element in the sentence.
Modifier placed too far from the word it is meant to describe.
Modifier that describes something not present in the sentence.

exercises.instruction: Rewrite to correct the misplaced modifier.
items: The young manager was walking the dog on the phone.
I heard about the product recall on the evening news.

exercises.instruction: Rewrite to correct the dangling modifier.
items: Riding the elevator, the lobby appeared below us.
To qualify for the role, three years of experience is required.

keyTakeaways: Misplaced modifiers create awkward sentences.
Place modifiers directly next to the words they describe.
Dangling modifiers describe something absent — add the missing subject.

sections.title: Commas
sections.content:
A **comma** indicates a pause or separates items.

## Six Uses

1. After introductory word or phrase: *However, the meeting was postponed.*
2. In a list: *We need paper, ink, and envelopes.*
3. Coordinating adjectives: *It was a clear, concise memo.*
4. Before conjunctions in compound sentences: *He submitted the report, but the deadline had passed.*
5. Around interrupting words: *The CEO, as expected, approved the budget.*
6. In dates, addresses, and letters: *May 4, 2023 / Dear Ms. Johnson, / Sincerely,*

keyTerms.definition: Punctuation indicating pause or separating items.
Series of adjectives before a noun, each describing it independently.

exercises.instruction: Add commas to correct these sentences.
items: Without a doubt hard work pays off.
Monday Tuesday and Wednesday are fully booked.
He missed the deadline but promised to deliver Friday.

keyTakeaways: Use commas after introductory words/phrases.
Commas separate list items and coordinating adjectives.
Comma before FANBOYS in compound sentence.

sections.title: Semicolons
sections.content:
A **semicolon** links two closely related independent clauses.

*The proposal was submitted; the client reviewed it immediately.*

## With Conjunctive Adverbs

| Function | Examples |
|----------|-----------|
| Addition | furthermore, moreover |
| Contrast | however, nevertheless |
| Cause/effect | therefore, consequently |

*The budget was approved; however, spending limits apply.*

## In Complex Lists

When items contain commas: *The conference includes Priya Sharma, CFO; David Lee, CTO; Ana Ruiz, CMO.*

keyTerms.definition: Links two closely related independent clauses.
Word showing relationship between two clauses (however, therefore) — used after semicolon.

exercises.instruction: Join these pairs with a semicolon and conjunctive adverb.
items: The presentation was excellent. The audience remained skeptical.
We submitted on time. The client approved it immediately.

keyTakeaways: Semicolons link closely related independent clauses.
Semicolon + conjunctive adverb + comma to show relationship.

sections.title: Colons
sections.content:
A **colon** introduces what follows. The preceding clause must be independent.

## Uses

- **List:** *The team will visit three cities: New York, Chicago, and Los Angeles.*
- **Quotation:** *The CEO said: 'We must cut costs by 15 percent.'*
- **Explanation:** *One issue stood out: the expense reports were incomplete.*
- **Business letter greeting:** *Dear Hiring Manager:*

## Do NOT Use After 'Such As'

**Incorrect:** *We offer services such as: design and printing.*
**Correct:** *We offer services such as design and printing.*

keyTerms.definition: Punctuation introducing a list, quotation, example, or explanation.

exercises.instruction: Add semicolons or colons where needed.
items: Don't give up you never know what tomorrow brings.
The boss's message was clear Lateness will not be tolerated.

keyTakeaways: Colon introduces lists, quotations, or explanations.
Independent clause must precede the colon.
Do not use colon after 'such as'.

sections.title: Quotes
sections.content:
**Quotation marks** enclose direct quotations and titles of short works.

**Direct quote:** *Carly said, "I'm not going back there."*
**Indirect quote (no marks):** *Carly said that she would not go back.*

## Rules

- Commas and periods go **inside** closing quotation mark
- Single quotation marks for quote within a quote
- Short work titles (articles, songs, poems) use quotation marks
- Long work titles (books, films) use italics

keyTerms.definition: Exact words someone said, enclosed in quotation marks.
Paraphrase of what was said; no quotation marks.
Used for a quotation within a quotation.

exercises.instruction: Add quotation marks where necessary.
items: Yasmin said, I don't feel like cooking tonight.
Did you hear her say you were the next Picasso?

keyTakeaways: Direct quotes require quotation marks; indirect quotes do not.
Commas and periods always go inside closing quotation mark.
Single quotes for a quote within a quote.

sections.title: Apostrophes
sections.content:
Apostrophes signal **possession** or mark **contractions**.

## Possessives
- Singular: add 's (the manager's report)
- Plural ending in -s: add ' only (the managers' meeting)
- Plural NOT ending in -s: add 's (the children's program)

## Common Errors
- **its** (possessive) vs **it's** (it is)
- **their** vs **they're** vs **there**
- Never use apostrophe for simple plurals: *reports* not *report's*

keyTerms.definition: Punctuation showing possession or forming contractions.
Shortened form using apostrophe to replace omitted letters.

exercises.instruction: Add apostrophes where needed.
items: The managers report is due Friday.
Its important to review the clients requirements.
Dont submit until youre satisfied.

keyTakeaways: Singular possessive = 's; plural ending in s = s'
its = possessive; it's = it is.
Never use apostrophe to form simple plurals.

sections.title: Parentheses
sections.content:
**Parentheses** enclose supplementary, nonessential information.

- Supplemental info: *The report (published in March) showed growth.*
- Abbreviations: *American Psychological Association (APA)*
- Numbers in formal documents: *twenty (20) business days*

Use sparingly — overuse clutters writing.

keyTerms.definition: Punctuation enclosing supplementary or nonessential information.

exercises.instruction: Add parentheses where appropriate.
items: The new software see the attached manual must be installed by Friday.

keyTakeaways: Parentheses enclose nonessential supplementary information.
Use sparingly to avoid cluttered prose.

sections.title: Dashes
learningObjectives: Use em dashes and en dashes correctly.
sections.content:
## Em Dash (--)

Indicates significant pause — stronger than comma, more informal than colon.

- Parenthetical: *The decision -- unanimous -- surprised everyone.*
- Introduce list: *Three things drove failure -- price, timing, trust.*

## En Dash (-)

Used for ranges: pages 10-25, years 2020-2024.

keyTerms.definition: Long dash indicating significant pause, emphasis, or parenthetical aside.
Medium dash used for numerical ranges.

exercises.instruction: Insert em dashes or en dashes as appropriate.
items: The report pages 12 28 cover financial projections.
Three factors drove the loss price, quality, and delivery.

keyTakeaways: Em dash creates strong pause or emphasis.
En dash indicates numerical ranges.

sections.title: Hyphens
sections.content:
## Compound Adjectives Before a Noun

Hyphenate before noun: *a well-written report, an up-to-date spreadsheet*
Do NOT hyphenate after linking verb: *The report was well written.*

## Compound Numbers
Hyphenate 21-99: *thirty-five employees*

## Self- Compounds
Almost always hyphenated: *self-confident, self-employed*

keyTerms.definition: Punctuation (-) connecting compound words or adjectives.
Two or more words functioning as single adjective before a noun.

exercises.instruction: Add or remove hyphens.
items: She is a well known consultant.
The consultant is well known in her field.
We hired twenty five new staff.

keyTakeaways: Hyphenate compound adjectives before nouns; not after linking verbs.
Hyphenate written numbers 21-99.

chapters.title: Working with Words: Which Word Is Right?

sections.title: Commonly Confused Words
learningObjectives: Identify and correctly use commonly confused words.
sections.content:
Many words sound alike but have completely different meanings.

| Word | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| accept | to receive |
| except | to exclude |
| affect | verb: to influence |
| effect | noun: result |
| their | possessive |
| there | place/introduces |
| they're | they are |
| its | possessive |
| it's | it is |
| your | possessive |
| you're | you are |
| then | time sequence |
| than | comparison |
| who | subject |
| whom | object |

keyTerms.definition: Words that sound the same but have different spellings and meanings.
Affect is usually a verb (to influence); effect is usually a noun (result).

exercises.instruction: Select the correct word.
items: The budget cuts will (affect/effect) every department.
(Their/There/They're) proposal was the strongest.
Please send to the person (who/whom) signed the contract.

keyTakeaways: Affect = verb; effect = noun.
Their/there/they're and its/it's are the most common errors.
Who = subject; whom = object.

sections.title: Spelling
sections.content:
## Key Rules

**i before e except after c:** *believe, receive, achieve, neighbor, weigh*

**Double final consonant** for one-syllable CVC before -ed/-ing: *run -> running, stop -> stopped*

**Silent e:** drop before vowel suffix, keep before consonant suffix: *write -> writing, safe -> safely*

## Common Business Misspellings
accomm*o*date, comm*i*ttee, ind*e*pendent, nec*e*ssary, rec*ei*ve, sep*a*rate

keyTerms.definition: Patterns governing correct letter order in words.

exercises.instruction: Correct the misspelled words.
items: The commitee will reconvene on Febuary 14th.
It is neccesary to recieve approval before proceeding.

keyTakeaways: i before e except after c has exceptions.
Double final consonant in one-syllable CVC words before vowel suffixes.
Spell-check misses homophone errors.

sections.title: Word Choice
learningObjectives: Use a dictionary and thesaurus effectively.
sections.content:
## Denotation vs. Connotation

**Denotation** = literal dictionary definition.
**Connotation** = emotional or cultural meaning.

| Word | Connotation |
|------|-------------|
| cheap | negative (low quality) |
| economical | neutral/positive |
| scrawny | negative (weakness) |
| lean | neutral/positive |

## Avoiding Cliches

*think outside the box, low-hanging fruit, move the needle, circle back* -- replace with specific language.

**Cliched:** *We need to move the needle on satisfaction.*
**Specific:** *We need to increase satisfaction scores by 10 points this quarter.*

keyTerms.definition: The literal dictionary definition of a word.
The emotional or cultural meaning attached to a word.
Overused expression that has lost impact and originality.

exercises.instruction: Replace the cliches with specific language.
items: We need to think outside the box on this.
Let's touch base before end of day.

keyTakeaways: Denotation is literal meaning; connotation is emotional meaning.
Replace cliches with specific, concrete language.

sections.title: Prefixes and Suffixes
learningObjectives: Use knowledge of affixes to expand vocabulary.
sections.content:
## Prefixes

| Prefix | Meaning | Example |
|--------|---------|----------|
| un- | not | unreliable |
| re- | again | renegotiate |
| pre- | before | prerequisite |
| mis- | wrong | misunderstand |
| dis- | not | disagree |
| co- | together | coworker |

## Suffixes

| Suffix | Function | Example |
|--------|----------|----------|
| -tion | noun | negotiation |
| -ment | noun | agreement |
| -ly | adverb | professionally |
| -able | capable of | negotiable |

keyTerms.definition: Word element added to beginning of root word to change meaning.
Word element added to end to change grammatical function.

exercises.instruction: Identify the prefix or suffix and explain how it changes the meaning.
items: disagree
renegotiate
management
finalize

keyTakeaways: Prefixes change meaning; suffixes change grammatical function.

sections.title: Synonyms and Antonyms
learningObjectives: Identify and use synonyms and antonyms.
sections.content:
**Synonym** = same/similar meaning: *begin: start, commence, initiate*
**Antonym** = opposite meaning: *profit vs. loss, approve vs. reject*

Always verify connotation before substituting a synonym. Longer synonyms are not inherently better: *use* not *utilize*.

keyTerms.definition: Word with same or similar meaning.
Word with opposite meaning.

exercises.instruction: Replace the underlined word with a more precise synonym.
items: The report was *good* and covered the key points.
We need to *fix* the errors before submitting.

keyTakeaways: Synonyms add variety; antonyms clarify contrast.
Always verify connotation before substituting.

sections.title: Using Context Clues
learningObjectives: Use context clues to determine word meaning.
sections.content:
## Four Types

1. **Definition:** Word defined immediately: *The CFO, or Chief Financial Officer, oversees finances.*
2. **Restatement:** Simplified version nearby: *The plan was feasible -- workable and achievable.*
3. **Contrast:** Opposite meaning via *but, however, although*: *While the first version was verbose, the revision was concise.*
4. **Inference:** Meaning implied by overall context.

keyTerms.definition: Surrounding text helping reveal meaning of unfamiliar words.
Opposite meaning signaled by but, however, unlike.

exercises.instruction: Use context clues to determine the meaning of the underlined word.
items: The contract was *null and void* -- it had no legal force and could not be enforced.
The CEO was *candid*; unlike her usual careful phrasing, she spoke with complete honesty.

keyTakeaways: Four context clue types: definition, restatement, contrast, inference.
Context clues speed up reading of technical documents.

sections.title: Word Order
sections.content:
English follows **Subject-Verb-Object (SVO)** order.

Adjectives precede nouns. Multiple adjectives follow this order: Opinion > Size > Age > Shape > Color > Origin > Material > Purpose + Noun.

Adverbs of frequency (*always, usually, often*) go before main verb, after be: *She always submits reports early.*

keyTerms.definition: Subject-Verb-Object -- standard English sentence order.

exercises.instruction: Reorder the scrambled words into correct English sentences.
items: report / the / submitted / manager / yesterday / the

keyTakeaways: English SVO order is mandatory.
Multiple adjectives follow a fixed order.

sections.title: Negative Statements
sections.content:
## With Auxiliary Verbs
*She is not available. / They have not submitted.*

## Without Auxiliary
Use do/does/did + not: *She does not agree. / They did not attend.*

## Double Negatives -- Avoid
**Incorrect:** *We don't have no budget.*
**Correct:** *We don't have any budget.* OR *We have no budget.*

keyTerms.definition: Two negative words in one clause -- incorrect in standard English.

exercises.instruction: Correct the double negatives.
items: We don't have no alternative.
He didn't say nothing about the changes.

keyTakeaways: Negatives use not after auxiliary, or do/does/did + not.
Double negatives are nonstandard -- avoid in formal writing.

sections.title: Count and Noncount Nouns and Articles
sections.content:
## Count Nouns
Can be counted; have singular and plural: *one report, two reports*

## Noncount Nouns
No plural form: *information, advice, feedback, equipment, software*

**Incorrect:** *She gave me three feedbacks.*
**Correct:** *She gave me three pieces of feedback.*

## Articles

| Article | Use |
|---------|-----|
| a | First mention, consonant sound |
| an | First mention, vowel sound |
| the | Specific or previously mentioned |
| (none) | General plural or noncount |

keyTerms.definition: Can be counted; has singular and plural forms.
Cannot be counted; has no plural form.
'the' -- used before specific nouns.
'a' or 'an' -- used before nonspecific singular count nouns.

exercises.instruction: Add the correct article (a, an, the, or nothing).
items: She submitted ___ report yesterday. ___ report was approved.
He has ___ MBA from Harvard.

keyTakeaways: Count nouns have plurals; noncount nouns do not.
A/an for first-mention; the for specific nouns.

sections.title: Modal Auxiliaries
learningObjectives: Use modal verbs correctly for ability, permission, and obligation.
sections.content:
Modal verbs: *can, could, may, might, shall, should, will, would, must, ought to*

Modals never add -s/-ed. Always followed by **base form**.

| Meaning | Modal | Example |
|---------|-------|---------|
| Ability | can | I can finalize this today. |
| Formal permission | may | May I reschedule? |
| Possibility | might | The client might request changes. |
| Strong obligation | must | You must sign before proceeding. |
| Advice | should | You should review the contract. |

**must not** = prohibition; **don't have to** = not necessary

keyTerms.definition: Verb expressing ability/permission/possibility/obligation.
Infinitive without 'to' -- always used after a modal.

exercises.instruction: Complete with the correct modal verb.
items: ___ I see the draft before it is submitted? (formal permission)
You ___ back up your data before the update. (strong obligation)

keyTakeaways: Modals never change form; always precede base verb.
must not = prohibition; don't have to = not necessary.

sections.title: Slang and Idioms
sections.content:
## Slang

Informal language -- avoid in professional writing.

| Slang | Professional |
|-------|-------------|
| awesome | excellent |
| ASAP | as soon as possible |
| totally | completely |

## Idioms

Expressions whose meaning differs from literal words.

| Idiom | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| a piece of cake | very easy |
| on pins and needles | very nervous |
| the sky is the limit | possibilities are endless |
| pulling your leg | making a joke |

keyTerms.definition: Informal nonstandard language -- avoid in professional writing.
Expression whose meaning differs from the literal words.

exercises.instruction: Rewrite this email replacing all slang with professional language.
items: Hey team! Our Q3 numbers are totally awesome. We killed it this quarter. Can you guys touch base ASAP about next steps?

keyTakeaways: Slang creates unprofessional impression.
Idioms confuse non-native speakers.
Use context clues to decode unfamiliar idioms.

chapters.title: Writing Paragraphs: Separating Ideas and Shaping Content

sections.title: Purpose, Audience, Tone, and Content
learningObjectives: Identify the four common academic purposes.
sections.content:
Three elements shape every paragraph: **purpose**, **audience**, and **tone**.

## Four Academic Purposes

- **Summary** -- condenses text to essential points
- **Analysis** -- separates into parts and examines relationships
- **Synthesis** -- combines multiple sources to create new understanding
- **Evaluation** -- judges value; presents opinion with evidence

## Audience Considerations

Demographics, education level, prior knowledge, expectations.

## Tone

Conveyed through word choice, sentence structure, and formality level.

keyTerms.definition: Reason writer creates document -- to summarize, analyze, synthesize, or evaluate.
Writer's attitude toward subject and audience.
Condenses text to essential points.
Separates material into parts and examines relationships.
Combines multiple sources to create new understanding.
Judges value and quality; presents opinion with evidence.

exercises.instruction: Identify the purpose of each paragraph.
items: This film runs twenty minutes too long and repeats emotional beats.
The report covers quarterly revenue, cost structure, and market share.

keyTakeaways: Four academic purposes: summarize, analyze, synthesize, evaluate.
Know audience demographics, education, prior knowledge, expectations.

sections.title: Effective Means for Writing a Paragraph
learningObjectives: Identify characteristics of a good topic sentence.
Identify the three parts of a developed paragraph.
sections.content:
A strong paragraph has three parts: **topic sentence**, **body**, and **concluding sentence**.

## Topic Sentence

Combines **main idea** with **controlling idea** (your specific stance).

**Weak:** *This paper is about rising tuition.*
**Strong:** *Rising tuition is pricing qualified students out of higher education.*

Five characteristics: accurate, main+controlling idea, clear, no supporting details, engaging.

## Transitions

| Function | Examples |
|----------|-----------|
| Addition | furthermore, moreover |
| Contrast | however, nevertheless |
| Cause/effect | therefore, consequently |
| Summary | in conclusion, in summary |

keyTerms.definition: Sentence controlling the main point of a paragraph.
Writer's specific stance within the topic sentence.
Develop, explain, or prove the topic sentence.
Connecting word showing logical relationships between ideas.

exercises.instruction: Choose the more effective topic sentence.
items: a) I will discuss the effects of poor communication. b) Poor internal communication costs companies millions in lost productivity annually.

keyTakeaways: Topic sentence = main idea + controlling idea.
Concluding sentence restates without introducing new ideas.

sections.title: Sentence Variety
learningObjectives: Identify ways to vary sentence structure.
sections.content:
## Techniques

- **Start with adverb:** *Confidently, she presented the findings.*
- **Start with prepositional phrase:** *During negotiations, all NDAs must be signed.*
- **Invert subject and verb:** *Attached is the revised proposal.*
- **-ing modifier:** *Reviewing the budget, the CFO found three discrepancies.*
- **Relative clause:** *The analyst, who joined last quarter, produced the best model.*
- **Appositive:** *Sarah Chen, our lead designer, presented the identity system.*

keyTerms.definition: Using different lengths, patterns, and structures to improve readability.
Clause beginning with who/which/that describing a noun.
Noun phrase placed next to another noun to rename or describe it.

exercises.instruction: Combine each pair using the technique indicated.
items: (appositive) Mariam Tahir is our CFO. She presented the annual budget.
(-ing modifier) He reviewed the proposal. He found several inconsistencies.

keyTakeaways: Varied sentence structure prevents monotony.
Combine sentences using modifiers, relative clauses, or appositives.

sections.title: Coordination and Subordination
learningObjectives: Combine sentences using coordination and subordination.
sections.content:
## Coordination

Joins two equal independent clauses using FANBOYS or conjunctive adverbs.

*The report was complete, but the presentation needed revision.*

**Conjunctive adverbs with semicolons:** *The project is behind; however, the quality is excellent.*

## Subordination

Joins unequal clauses, emphasizing one over the other.

*Although the report was late, the data was accurate.*

Common subordinating conjunctions: *although, because, since, unless, if, when, while*

**Punctuation:** Comma after dependent clause when it comes first.

keyTerms.definition: Joining two equal independent clauses using FANBOYS or conjunctive adverbs.
Joining a dependent clause to a main clause showing unequal importance.
FANBOYS: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so.
Joins dependent clause to main clause (although, because, since, unless).

exercises.instruction: Join using a coordinating conjunction or conjunctive adverb.
items: The client approved the concept. Production can begin immediately.

exercises.instruction: Join using a subordinating conjunction.
items: The merger failed. The regulatory approval was denied.

keyTakeaways: Coordination gives equal weight; subordination emphasizes one clause.
FANBOYS preceded by comma; conjunctive adverbs preceded by semicolon.

sections.title: Parallelism
sections.content:
**Parallelism** uses the same grammatical structure for related elements.

**Faulty:** *The manager is responsible for hiring staff, to train employees, and budget oversight.*
**Parallel:** *The manager is responsible for hiring staff, training employees, and overseeing the budget.*

## With Correlative Conjunctions

Both parts of *either...or, neither...nor, not only...but also* must match:
**Faulty:** *We can either reduce costs or increasing revenue.*
**Parallel:** *We can either reduce costs or increase revenue.*

keyTerms.definition: Using the same grammatical structure for related elements.
Inconsistent grammatical structures in a list or paired construction.
Paired conjunctions (either...or, neither...nor) requiring parallel structures.

exercises.instruction: Correct the faulty parallelism.
items: The new system will improve accuracy, reduce costs, and the team will work faster.
We can either postpone the launch or we could reduce the feature set.

keyTakeaways: Items in lists and paired clauses must use matching grammatical forms.

chapters.title: The Writing Process: How Do I Begin?

sections.title: Apply Prewriting Models
learningObjectives: Use prewriting strategies to choose and narrow a topic.
sections.content:
Writing is a **process**: Prewriting > Outlining > Drafting > Revising > Editing.

## Six Prewriting Strategies

1. Using experience and observations
2. Reading
3. **Freewriting** -- write continuously for 3-5 minutes without stopping
4. **Asking 5WH questions** -- Who? What? Where? When? Why? How?
5. **Brainstorming** -- list every idea without evaluation
6. **Idea mapping** -- circles connected by lines; visual approach

keyTerms.definition: Stage transferring abstract thoughts into concrete ideas before drafting.
Writing continuously for set time without stopping or editing.
Rapidly listing all ideas without evaluation.
Who, What, Where, When, Why, How -- used to explore a topic.

exercises.instruction: Choose a business topic and complete a 5-minute freewrite. Then identify three potential essay angles.

keyTakeaways: Writing is a process: prewrite, outline, draft, revise, edit.
Narrow from broad to specific topic before outlining.

sections.title: Outlining
learningObjectives: Construct a topic outline and a sentence outline.
sections.content:
An outline is the skeleton of your document.

## Organization Methods

| Method | When to Use |
|--------|-------------|
| Chronological | Narratives, processes, histories |
| Spatial | Descriptions of places or objects |
| Order of Importance | Persuasive writing, rankings |

## Formal Outline Structure

- Roman numerals (I, II, III) = main points
- Capital letters (A, B, C) = supporting details
- Arabic numerals (1, 2, 3) = sub-details

Every level must have at least two entries.

keyTerms.definition: Structured plan organizing main points before drafting.
One sentence presenting the essay's controlling idea.
Preliminary thesis guiding the outline; refined as writing progresses.

exercises.instruction: Write a working thesis for each topic.
items: The impact of remote work on team communication
Why business emails are often misunderstood

keyTakeaways: Choose organization based on purpose.
Every outline level must have at least two entries.

sections.title: Drafting
sections.content:
A first draft is **complete but unpolished**.

## Strategies

- Start with the section you know best
- Don't edit while drafting
- Keep purpose and audience visible

## Elements of a First Draft

1. Introduction -- hook + context + thesis
2. Body paragraphs -- topic sentence, supporting sentences, concluding sentence
3. Conclusion -- restate thesis, synthesize, provide closure
4. Title -- drafted last

keyTerms.definition: Complete but unpolished version -- not the final product.
Opening with hook, context, and thesis statement.
Closing that restates thesis and provides closure without new arguments.

exercises.instruction: Write an opening paragraph (hook + context + thesis) for a memo proposing a new remote work policy.

keyTakeaways: First drafts are complete but unpolished -- don't edit while drafting.
Business documents benefit from front-loaded topic sentences.

sections.title: Revising and Editing
sections.content:
**Revising** = rethinking content and structure (do first).
**Editing** = correcting grammar and punctuation (do second).

## ARMS Revision Strategy

- **A**dd -- missing information, evidence, transitions
- **R**emove -- redundant or off-topic content
- **M**ove -- restructure for better logic
- **S**ubstitute -- weak words, vague claims

Reading your draft **aloud** catches awkward phrasing that the eye skips over.

keyTerms.definition: Making substantive changes to content, structure, and argument.
Correcting surface errors in grammar, spelling, and punctuation.
Add, Remove, Move, Substitute -- systematic approach to revision.

exercises.instruction: Apply the ARMS strategy to a paragraph. Identify one change in each category.

keyTakeaways: Revise for content and structure before editing for surface errors.
ARMS = Add, Remove, Move, Substitute.
Read aloud to catch problems invisible to the eye.

chapters.title: Writing Essays: From Start to Finish

sections.title: Developing a Strong, Clear Thesis Statement
sections.content:
A **thesis statement** is specific, arguable, and supportable.

**Weak:** *Technology affects how we communicate.*
**Strong:** *The rise of asynchronous messaging tools has reduced spontaneous collaboration, increasing productivity but decreasing team cohesion.*

## Common Errors

- Too obvious: unargued facts
- Announcement: 'In this essay, I will explain...'
- Too broad: can't be covered in the space available

Thesis goes at the **end of the introduction**.

keyTerms.definition: Specific, arguable sentence presenting the essay's controlling idea.
Preliminary thesis guiding drafting; refined as writing progresses.

exercises.instruction: Evaluate as weak or strong. Improve the weak ones.
items: Social media has changed communication.
Open-plan offices reduce deep work by exposing employees to constant ambient noise and visual interruptions.
This essay will discuss problems with open-plan offices.

keyTakeaways: Thesis must be specific, arguable, and supportable.
Avoid announcements and overly broad claims.

sections.title: Writing Body Paragraphs
learningObjectives: Structure effective body paragraphs using PIE.
sections.content:
Each body paragraph develops one main point using **PIE**:

- **P -- Point:** Topic sentence stating the main argument
- **I -- Illustration:** Specific evidence (fact, statistic, quote, example)
- **E -- Explanation:** Why the evidence supports your point

**Example:**
*P: Remote workers report higher job satisfaction.*
*I: A Stanford study found remote employees were 13% more productive.*
*E: This suggests autonomy drives both output and retention.*

keyTerms.definition: Point (topic sentence), Illustration (evidence), Explanation (analysis).
Explanation of why evidence supports the argument -- the E in PIE.

exercises.instruction: Write a PIE paragraph on: the value of plain language in business.

keyTakeaways: PIE: Point (claim), Illustration (evidence), Explanation (analysis).
Analysis is the most important and most often missing element.

sections.title: Organizing Your Writing
sections.content:
## Three Main Patterns

- **Chronological** -- by time; for narratives, histories, processes
- **Spatial** -- by physical location; for descriptions
- **Order of Importance** -- by significance; for persuasive writing

Longer documents often use different patterns in different sections.

keyTerms.definition: Organizing ideas by time sequence.
Organizing ideas by physical arrangement.
Organizing ideas from most to least significant.

exercises.instruction: Which pattern would you choose and why?
items: A business case for adopting new project management software.
Instructions for submitting a reimbursement request.

keyTakeaways: Choose organization based on natural relationship between ideas.
Transitions signal which pattern you are using.

sections.title: Writing Introductory and Concluding Paragraphs
sections.content:
## Introduction: Three Parts

**Hook > Context > Thesis**

Hook strategies: startling statistic, provocative question, vivid anecdote, bold claim.
Avoid: 'In this essay, I will...' / 'Since the beginning of time...'

## Conclusion: Three Parts

**Thesis restatement (new words) > Summary > Closing move**

Closing moves: broader significance, call to action, prediction, memorable final thought.
Never introduce new arguments in the conclusion.

keyTerms.definition: Opening device capturing reader attention -- statistic, question, anecdote, or bold claim.

exercises.instruction: Write an introduction for a proposal recommending plain language in corporate communications.
Write a conclusion that restates thesis, synthesizes points, and ends with a call to action.

keyTakeaways: Introduction: hook + context + thesis.
Conclusion: restate thesis + synthesize + closing move.
Never introduce new arguments in the conclusion.

sections.title: Oral versus Written Communication
learningObjectives: Explain similarities and differences between oral and written communication.
sections.content:
Both forms share eight communication elements: source, receiver, message, channel, feedback, environment, context, interference.

## The Key Difference: Asynchronous

Written communication is typically **asynchronous** -- no real-time interaction.
- No immediate feedback
- Words must stand alone without vocal tone or gestures
- Writer must anticipate reader questions and interpretations

Every document represents you in your absence.

keyTerms.definition: Occurs at different times, without real-time interaction.
Medium through which a message travels from source to receiver.
Anything blocking, distorting, or disrupting the communication process.

exercises.instruction: For each scenario, identify source, channel, and likely interference.
items: A manager emails a remote team member about a deadline change.
A company publishes a press release on its website.

keyTakeaways: Oral and written share eight communication elements.
Written communication is typically asynchronous.
Every document represents you in your absence.

sections.title: Good Writing
learningObjectives: Identify qualities of good business writing.
sections.content:
## Six Qualities

1. Follows the rules
2. Is easy to read
3. Attracts the reader
4. Meets reader expectations
5. Is clear and concise
6. Is efficient and effective

## Rhetorical Elements

**Logos** -- logical appeal: facts and structured reasoning
**Ethos** -- credibility appeal: expertise and trustworthiness
**Pathos** -- emotional appeal: connection to reader values

keyTerms.definition: Rhetorical appeal to logic and reason.
Rhetorical appeal to credibility and character.
Rhetorical appeal to emotion and reader values.

exercises.instruction: Identify whether each sentence uses logos, ethos, or pathos.
items: Studies across 15 countries show clear communication reduces project failure by 30%.
As a 20-year veteran, I can say this approach works.
Imagine explaining to your client why the shipment is six weeks late -- again.

keyTakeaways: Good writing: follows rules, easy to read, attracts reader, clear, concise, effective.
Balance logos, ethos, and pathos for maximum persuasion.

sections.title: Style in Written Communication
learningObjectives: Choose the appropriate writing style for a given context.
sections.content:
## Three Styles

- **Colloquial** -- informal, slang; only between close colleagues
- **Casual** -- everyday language; internal team messages
- **Formal** -- professional vocabulary; client correspondence, reports, proposals

## Active vs. Passive Voice

**Active:** *The manager approved the budget.* -- clear, direct
**Passive:** *The budget was approved by the manager.* -- diffuses agency

Use active voice as default.

keyTerms.definition: Professional expression with precise vocabulary and complete sentences.
Subject performs the action.
Subject receives the action.

exercises.instruction: Rewrite in formal style.
items: Hey -- we totally dropped the ball on this one, sorry.

exercises.instruction: Convert passive to active voice.
items: The report was completed by the analyst last Friday.
Mistakes were made in the budget calculation.

keyTakeaways: Match style to audience and context.
External communication requires formal register.
Active voice is clearer and more direct than passive.

sections.title: Principles of Written Communication
learningObjectives: Understand legal implications of business writing.
sections.content:
## Use Concrete, Specific Language

**Vague:** *We will improve customer service.*
**Specific:** *We will reduce average call wait time from 4 minutes to 90 seconds by Q3.*

## Legal Responsibility

**Libel** -- written defamation: false statements damaging someone's reputation.
- Never state opinions as facts
- Qualify claims: 'In our view...' vs. asserting facts about competitors

**Copyright** -- always cite sources; never present others' work as your own.

keyTerms.definition: Written defamation -- a false statement damaging someone's reputation.
Legal right of an author to control use and reproduction of their original work.

exercises.instruction: Identify which statements could expose a company to libel claims. Rewrite them safely.
items: Our competitor's product has caused injuries the company is covering up.
In our opinion, our service outperforms others in the market.

keyTakeaways: Use concrete, specific language.
Libel and copyright are real legal risks in business writing.
State opinions as opinions, not facts.

sections.title: Overcoming Barriers to Effective Written Communication
sections.content:
## Types of Barriers

- **Physical** -- poor formatting, dense paragraphs
- **Language** -- jargon, undefined acronyms, idioms
- **Emotional** -- stress, defensiveness, distrust of sender
- **Organizational** -- information silos, wrong distribution list

## Strategies

- Define all acronyms on first use: *Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP)*
- Use plain language: *use* not *utilize*, *buy* not *procure*
- Proofread -- errors undermine credibility
- Write for global audiences: avoid idioms, be explicit

keyTerms.definition: Anything preventing a message from being received and understood as intended.
Clear, direct writing avoiding unnecessary complexity.

exercises.instruction: Rewrite this paragraph to remove language barriers for a non-specialist client.
items: We need to finalize the SOW for the ERP implementation before we can proceed with the UAT phase.

keyTakeaways: Define all acronyms on first use.
Plain language overcomes most language barriers.

sections.title: Think, Then Write: Writing Preparation
learningObjectives: Explain why preparation is important in business writing.
sections.content:
## Critical Thinking in Writing

Critical thinking = self-directed, disciplined evaluation of evidence.

**Confirmation bias** -- seeking information that confirms existing beliefs. Combat it by gathering evidence from a range of sources.

## Overcoming Fear of Writing

Three sources of writing fear:
1. Negative orientation -- build positive associations through small successes
2. Risk of failure -- embrace rough drafts as normal process
3. Fear of the unknown -- study examples of the document type before writing

keyTerms.definition: Self-directed, disciplined thinking that evaluates evidence objectively.
Seeking information confirming existing beliefs while ignoring contradictory evidence.

exercises.instruction: Identify one example of confirmation bias in a business context and explain how a writer could avoid it.

keyTakeaways: Confirmation bias weakens arguments -- seek diverse sources.
Rough drafts are a normal and expected part of the process.

sections.title: A Planning Checklist for Business Messages
learningObjectives: Use a planning checklist before writing.
sections.content:
Before writing any business message, answer:

1. What is my purpose?
2. Who is my primary audience?
3. Who is my secondary audience?
4. What action do I want the reader to take?
5. What format is appropriate?
6. What tone is appropriate?
7. What is the deadline?

Planning time = saved revision time.

keyTerms.definition: Structured set of questions answered before writing to ensure purposeful communication.

exercises.instruction: Complete the planning checklist for this scenario: Tell your team the project deadline has moved up by one week.

keyTakeaways: Answer all planning questions before drafting.
Planning prevents revision.

sections.title: Ethics, Plagiarism, and Reliable Sources
sections.content:
## Types of Plagiarism

- Direct -- copying word for word without citation
- Mosaic -- patching phrases with minor word changes
- Paraphrase without citation
- Self-plagiarism -- submitting the same work twice

## The CRAAP Test

| Letter | Question |
|--------|-----------|
| Currency | How recent? |
| Relevance | Does it address your topic? |
| Authority | Who wrote it? |
| Accuracy | Are claims supported by evidence? |
| Purpose | Why was it written? |

keyTerms.definition: Presenting another person's words or ideas as your own without attribution.
Currency, Relevance, Authority, Accuracy, Purpose -- framework for evaluating sources.

exercises.instruction: Apply the CRAAP test to evaluate these sources.
items: A 2023 article in the Harvard Business Review by a communication researcher.
A personal blog post from 2019 with no author listed.

keyTakeaways: Cite all ideas not your own.
CRAAP test: Currency, Relevance, Authority, Accuracy, Purpose.

sections.title: Organization
learningObjectives: Organize writing logically using deductive and inductive patterns.
sections.content:
## Deductive vs. Inductive

**Deductive:** thesis first, then evidence. Best for most business writing.
**Inductive:** evidence first, conclusion last. Use when audience might resist.

## Logical Flow

Each sentence connects to the one before and leads to the one after.

**Test:** Cover your conclusion and try to predict it from the body. If you can, your organization is working.

keyTerms.definition: General-to-specific: thesis first, then supporting evidence.
Specific-to-general: evidence first, then conclusion.
Smooth, coherent progression from one idea to the next.

exercises.instruction: Should this use deductive or inductive organization? Explain.
items: A proposal recommending outsourcing to a CEO who strongly prefers in-house operations.
A quarterly performance update to a board that expects summaries first.

keyTakeaways: Deductive: thesis first (most business documents).
Inductive: builds to conclusion when audience resistance expected.

sections.title: Making an Argument
sections.content:
Every business document that recommends or analyzes is making an argument.

## Elements of a Strong Argument

- **Claim** -- central assertion (thesis)
- **Evidence** -- specific, verifiable facts
- **Reasoning** -- logical explanation connecting evidence to claim
- **Rebuttal** -- acknowledge and respond to counterarguments

## Logical Fallacies to Avoid

- **Ad hominem** -- attacking the person, not the argument
- **Straw man** -- misrepresenting the opposing view
- **False dichotomy** -- presenting only two options when more exist

keyTerms.definition: The central assertion of an argument.
Specific, verifiable information supporting a claim.
Error in reasoning that invalidates an argument.

exercises.instruction: Identify the logical fallacy in each example.
items: We can either reduce costs or lose the company -- no other option.
The CEO said this approach is best, so it must be right.

keyTakeaways: Strong arguments: claim + evidence + reasoning + rebuttal.
Address counterarguments -- it strengthens your position.
Avoid logical fallacies: ad hominem, straw man, false dichotomy.

sections.title: General Revision Points to Consider
sections.content:
Revision is rethinking at the level of argument and structure.

## Macro vs. Micro Revision

**Macro** (do first): content, structure, argument, logic
**Micro** (do second): paragraphs, sentences, word choice
**Editing** (do last): grammar, spelling, punctuation

## Revision Checklist

- Does the thesis appear clearly and early?
- Is the organization logical?
- Does each section connect to the main point?
- Is evidence sufficient and relevant?
- Does the conclusion synthesize, not just repeat?

Put the draft aside before revising -- fresh eyes catch more.

keyTerms.definition: Big-picture changes to content, structure, and argument.
Sentence-level changes to word choice and paragraph construction.

exercises.instruction: This paragraph needs revision. Identify what is wrong and rewrite it.
items: Communication is very important in business. A lot of companies have problems because of this. We should all try to communicate better. In conclusion, communication matters a lot.

keyTakeaways: Revise macro (content/structure) before micro (sentences/words).
Create distance between drafting and revising.

sections.title: Proofreading and Design Evaluation
sections.content:
## Proofreading Strategies

1. **Read aloud** -- catches awkward phrasing and missing words
2. **Read backward** -- sentence by sentence from end to beginning
3. **Print it** -- errors more visible on paper
4. **Take a break first** -- fresh eyes catch more
5. **Spell-check is just a starting point** -- misses homophones (their/there, its/it's)

## Design Evaluation

- Font: 11-12pt; consistent throughout
- White space: adequate margins prevent visual fatigue
- Headers: logical hierarchy; consistent formatting
- Page numbers required for multi-page documents

keyTerms.definition: Final check for surface errors -- after all revisions are complete.
Blank space on a page improving readability and visual clarity.

exercises.instruction: Proofread this business email and list all errors.
items: Dear Ms johnson Thank you for youre email regarding the contract. I have reviewed its terms and have a few concern. Their are three clauses that needs to be revised.

keyTakeaways: Proofread after all revisions -- not before.
Reading aloud catches what silent reading misses.
Spell-check misses homophone errors.

sections.title: Text, E-mail, and Netiquette
sections.content:
## Business Email Best Practices

- **Subject line** -- specific and informative: *Q3 Budget Approval Needed by Friday*
- **Salutation** -- match formality: *Dear Ms. Johnson:* (external), *Hi David,* (internal)
- **Body** -- lead with main point; 3 paragraphs max
- Reply within 24 hours
- Never send in anger -- draft, wait, reread
- Use Reply All only when everyone genuinely needs your response
- Never use ALL CAPS

## Netiquette

Treat others online as you would face to face. Never write what you would not want read publicly or by your employer.

keyTerms.definition: Accepted etiquette and protocols for communication on the internet.
Brief, descriptive heading communicating the message's purpose.
Automatically appended block with name, title, and contact information.

exercises.instruction: Rewrite this email professionally.
items: hey team just wanted to touch base about the johnson thing. i still havent heard back which is annoying. can you follow up asap. thx

exercises.instruction: Evaluate this subject line and suggest an improvement.
items: Subject: hi
Subject: IMPORTANT PLEASE READ

keyTakeaways: Subject lines must be specific and informative.
Reply within 24 hours; never send in anger.
Netiquette: treat digital communication with the same care as face-to-face.

sections.title: Memorandums and Letters
learningObjectives: Discuss the purpose and format of a memo.
Describe the fifteen parts of a business letter.
sections.content:
## Memos

Internal document communicating policies or official information.

**Format:** TO: / FROM: / DATE: / SUBJECT: + Declaration + Discussion + Summary

State purpose in the first sentence; objective tone; memos may have legal standing.

## Business Letters

External documents -- formal, on letterhead.

**Fifteen elements:** Return address, Date, Reference (Re:), Delivery method, Recipient note, Salutation, Introduction, Body, Conclusion, Close, Signature, Typed name, Preparation line, Enclosures, CC

Use colon after business salutation: *Dear Ms. Kim:*

keyTerms.definition: Brief internal document communicating policies or official business.
Unofficial informal communication network within an organization.
Pre-printed stationery displaying organization name, logo, and contact information.

exercises.instruction: Write a one-paragraph memo informing staff the office closes at noon on Friday. Include all four header elements.

keyTakeaways: Memos for internal; letters for external communication.
Memos: state purpose first.
Both represent the organization and may have legal standing.

sections.title: Business Proposal
learningObjectives: Describe elements of a business proposal.
sections.content:
A **business proposal** persuades an audience to accept a solution or award a contract.

## Standard Structure

| Section | Purpose |
|---------|---------|
| Executive Summary | 1-2 paragraph overview |
| Background | History and relationship |
| Proposal | Who, what, where, when, why, how |
| Market Analysis | Competitive landscape |
| Benefits | Specific value to client |
| Timeline | Milestones with dates |
| Budget | Costs and ROI |
| Conclusion | Restate strengths; call to action |

Every effective proposal uses ethos (credentials), pathos (pain points), and logos (data).

keyTerms.definition: Document persuading an audience to accept a solution or award a contract.
1-2 paragraph overview summarizing key points and value proposition.
Formal document inviting vendors to submit proposals.

exercises.instruction: Write an executive summary (2 paragraphs) for a proposal to implement a new internal communication platform.

keyTakeaways: Effective proposals use ethos, pathos, and logos.
Executive summary is the most-read section.
Be specific: vague claims lose proposals.

sections.title: Report
learningObjectives: Discuss the main parts of a report.
sections.content:
## Two Main Types

**Informational** -- presents facts without analysis.
**Analytical** -- presents data plus analysis, conclusions, and recommendations.

## Standard Structure

Title Page > Abstract/Executive Summary > Introduction > Body (Background, Methodology, Results, Analysis) > Conclusion > References > Appendices

Every report answers: Who? What? Where? When? Why? How?

keyTerms.definition: Presents facts without analysis -- no conclusions or recommendations.
Presents data plus analysis, conclusions, and recommendations.
Brief summary at beginning highlighting key topics, methods, and findings.

exercises.instruction: Classify as informational or analytical and explain why.
items: A weekly sales summary showing units sold by region.
A study analyzing why sales fell 20% in Q2, identifying causes, and recommending action.

keyTakeaways: Informational: facts only; analytical: facts + analysis + recommendations.
All reports answer who, what, where, when, why, how.

sections.title: Resume
sections.content:
A **resume** summarizes education, skills, and experience. Its one purpose: get an interview.

## Five Types

| Type | Best for |
|------|-----------|
| Reverse chronological | Steady career progression |
| Functional | Career changers |
| Combination | Experienced professionals |
| Targeted | Competitive positions |
| Scannable | Companies using ATS |

## Scannable Resume Tips

Mirror job description language; standard fonts; no tables or graphics (confuse ATS software).

keyTerms.definition: Document summarizing education, skills, and experience for employers.
Listing experiences starting with most recent, working backward.
Resume formatted for ATS software -- no graphics, standard fonts, keyword-optimized.

exercises.instruction: Which is stronger and why?
items: a) Responsible for handling customer complaints. b) Resolved 95% of complaints within 24 hours, achieving highest satisfaction score in the department (Q2 2023).

keyTakeaways: Resume goal: earn an interview.
Mirror job description language for ATS optimization.
Accomplishment bullets should be specific and quantified.

sections.title: Sales Message
sections.content:
A **sales message** intrigues, informs, persuades, calls to action, and closes.

## Five-Part Structure

| Part | Function |
|------|-----------|
| Attention Statement | Hook immediately |
| Introduction | Build interest; establish relevance |
| Body | Credibility + benefits + handle objections |
| Conclusion | Summarize value; specific call to action |
| Residual Message | What you want them to remember |

**Sell benefits, not features:**
Feature: *The platform has 99.9% uptime.*
Benefit: *You will never miss a client deadline because of a system outage.*

keyTerms.definition: Persuasive communication moving a reader toward a purchase or action.
What the buyer gains -- the outcome that motivates purchase.
Specific, clear request directing reader to take a next step.

exercises.instruction: Convert these features into benefits.
items: Our software processes requests in 0.3 seconds.
The contract includes 24/7 phone support.

keyTakeaways: Sell benefits not features.
Lead with strongest benefit; one call to action per message.

chapters.title: APA and MLA Documentation and Formatting

sections.title: Formatting a Research Paper
sections.content:
## APA Format (Social Sciences)

12pt Times New Roman, double-spaced, 1-inch margins
- Title page, abstract (150-250 words), running head
- In-text: (Author, Year, p. XX)
- References page at end

## MLA Format (Humanities)

12pt Times New Roman, double-spaced, 1-inch margins
- Header: last name + page number
- No separate title page
- In-text: (Author Page)
- Works Cited page at end

keyTerms.definition: American Psychological Association format -- used in social sciences.
Modern Language Association format -- used in humanities.
150-250 word summary at beginning of APA papers.

exercises.instruction: What are the three most important formatting differences between APA and MLA?

keyTakeaways: APA for social sciences; MLA for humanities.
APA in-text: (Author, Year); MLA: (Author Page).

sections.title: Citing and Referencing Techniques
sections.content:
Cite every time you use information from a source -- quoted, paraphrased, or summarized.

**APA:** (Author, Year, p. XX) for direct quotes; (Author, Year) for paraphrases
**MLA:** (Author Page)

## Signal Phrases

*According to Lee (2022), ... / Lee argues that ... / Research by Kim (2021) demonstrates ...*

## Block Quotations

APA: 40+ words -- indent 0.5 inches, no quotation marks
MLA: 4+ lines -- indent 1 inch, no quotation marks

keyTerms.definition: Parenthetical reference within paper body pointing to full bibliography entry.
Phrase introducing a source (According to..., Smith argues...).
Lengthy quote formatted separately: indented, no quotation marks.

exercises.instruction: Write an in-text citation in both APA and MLA formats.
items: Direct quote from page 23 of a book by Wilson published in 2020.

keyTakeaways: Cite direct quotes, paraphrases, statistics, and specific arguments.
Signal phrases integrate citations smoothly.

sections.title: Creating a References Section
learningObjectives: Create APA References and MLA Works Cited pages.
sections.content:
## APA References Page

Title: **References** (centered, bold)
Alphabetical, double-spaced, hanging indent.

**Book:** Author, A. A. (Year). *Title*. Publisher.
**Journal:** Author, A. A. (Year). Article title. *Journal Name, Volume*(Issue), pages. DOI

## MLA Works Cited

Title: **Works Cited** (centered)
Alphabetical, double-spaced, hanging indent.

**Book:** Author Last, First. *Title*. Publisher, Year.
**Journal:** Author. 'Article Title.' *Journal Name*, vol. #, no. #, Year, pp. #-#.

keyTerms.definition: APA bibliography -- alphabetical, hanging indent.
MLA bibliography -- alphabetical, hanging indent.
First line flush left; all subsequent lines indented.
Digital Object Identifier -- permanent URL for academic journal articles.

exercises.instruction: Format in APA References format.
items: Book: Writing for Results by Sally Jones, McGraw-Hill, 2019.

keyTakeaways: APA = References; MLA = Works Cited.
Both use alphabetical order and hanging indent.

sections.title: Using Modern Language Association (MLA) Style
learningObjectives: Apply MLA formatting and citation style.
sections.content:
MLA is standard in literature, language, and the humanities.

## In-Text Citations

**(Author Page)** -- no comma: *(McLean 247)*

## Works Cited -- MLA 9th Edition

The **container concept**: every source exists within a larger container (journal, anthology, website).

**Article:** Kim, Sarah. 'Plain Language in Business.' *Business Writing Today*, vol. 4, no. 2, 2021, pp. 12-18.

**Website:** U.S. Department of Labor. 'Plain Language Guidelines.' *DOL.gov*, 15 Mar. 2022, www.dol.gov/plain.

keyTerms.definition: Humanities citation format -- in-text (Author Page), Works Cited bibliography.
MLA 9th: larger publication holding a source (journal, anthology, website).

exercises.instruction: Write MLA Works Cited entries.
items: A webpage titled Grammar in the Workplace on PlainLanguage.gov, updated June 10, 2023.

keyTakeaways: MLA in-text: (Author Page) -- no comma.
Works Cited uses container concept.
